Cocktail shaker sort.use: A teaching comparison with bubble sort when small values need to travel left as well as large values right.

Comb sort.use: A study of whether moving distant inversions early reduces later adjacent swaps on the same input.
Comb sort.average: Depends on input distribution and the shrink policy; the displayed quadratic worst-case bound is not an average.

Gnome sort.use: A compact way to express insertion-like repair using a cursor that walks forward and backward.

Shellsort.use: An array sort with constant auxiliary storage, when the selected gap sequence suits the workload.
Shellsort.average: Depends on the gap sequence as well as the distribution of inputs.

Bottom-up merge sort.use: A merge-based implementation that should use iterative passes rather than recursive calls.

Natural merge sort.use: A collection already organised into ascending runs, where recognising those runs avoids rebuilding all order.
Natural merge sort.average: Depends on the number and lengths of runs and the merge schedule.
Natural merge sort.cost: O(n log r) with pairwise merge passes; O(n) for one run

Three-way quicksort.use: A list containing many repeated keys, where equal values can be removed from further recursive sorting.

Dual-pivot quicksort.use: An implementation study of partitioning into three regions and the memory scans those partitions require.
Dual-pivot quicksort.average: Depends on pivot selection, duplicates and the surrounding hybrid implementation.

Smoothsort.use: A memory-constrained setting where adaptation to existing order is worth more involved heap bookkeeping.
Smoothsort.average: Depends on pre-existing order; its best and worst bounds describe different ends of that range.

Tree sort.use: Records being inserted into an ordered search structure that will later be traversed in key order.
Tree sort.average: Depends on the tree’s balancing policy and insertion order.

Tournament sort.use: Repeatedly selecting the next record while retaining comparisons from earlier rounds in a tournament tree.
Tournament sort.average: O(n log n) is also an upper bound on average work in the usual tournament-tree model.

Cycle sort.average: Depends on how destination ranks are obtained; the common comparison-ranked variant spends quadratic work finding them.

Patience sorting.average: Depends on the pile structure and the search/extraction implementation; the efficient version has O(n log n) total work.

Strand sort.use: A linked-list exercise in removing increasing subsequences and merging them into an accumulated output.
Strand sort.average: Depends on how long the extracted strands are and how they are merged.

Ford–Johnson / merge-insertion.use: Small inputs whose comparisons are expensive enough to justify a carefully scheduled insertion process.
Ford–Johnson / merge-insertion.average: The classic objective is worst-case comparison count; average comparisons require an input model.

MSD radix sort.average: Depends on shared prefixes, key lengths, radix and how each recursive bucket is processed.

Bucket sort.use: Numeric keys with a known useful distribution, so ordered ranges can divide the work into small local sorts.
Bucket sort.average: Expected linear work needs an appropriate distribution and bucket count; a crowded bucket changes the cost.

Histogram sort.use: A distribution pipeline that must know each bucket’s size before assigning contiguous output space.
Histogram sort.average: Depends on bucket occupancy and the method used to finish each bucket.

Pigeonhole sort.use: Records whose integer keys occupy a small range and can be collected into one container per possible key.
Pigeonhole sort.average: The usual scan-and-collect procedure costs O(n + k) for all inputs in the stated key range.

American flag sort.use: Digit-based grouping where a full second record array is undesirable and stability is not required.
American flag sort.average: Depends on key lengths, radix and the distribution of prefixes.

Flashsort.use: Numeric data where interpolation yields useful classes and the subsequent cleanup stays inexpensive.
Flashsort.average: Its favourable distribution assumptions govern class balance and cleanup work.

Spreadsort.use: Numeric or string keys for which radix partitioning can cooperate with comparison-sort fallbacks.
Spreadsort.average: Depends on the key representation and the hybrid’s choice between distribution and comparisons.

Introsort.average: Input and pivot strategy affect typical work; the O(n log n) worst bound also bounds average work.

Timsort.average: Depends on existing run lengths, repeated keys and the merge policy.

Powersort.average: Depends on the lengths of detected runs; the merge schedule is designed to use that structure.

Peeksort.use: A run-aware stable sort whose merge schedule is constructed recursively around runs near a midpoint.
Peeksort.average: Depends on the run-length structure discovered around recursive midpoints.

Multiway Powersort.use: An investigation of merging several existing runs together to reduce data transfers across merge levels.
Multiway Powersort.average: Depends on run lengths and merge arity; the fixed-arity worst bound also bounds average work.

GrailSort.use: Stable array sorting when an external record buffer is unavailable and internal block management is acceptable.
GrailSort.average: Input structure and internal buffer availability affect work within the stated worst-case bound.

WikiSort.use: A stable block-merge implementation for exploring the cost of replacing large buffers with rotations and searches.
WikiSort.average: Rotations, searches, duplicates and optional caching affect work within its worst-case bound.

Pattern-defeating quicksort.use: General-purpose unstable sorting that should recognise or disrupt patterns leading to bad partitions.
Pattern-defeating quicksort.average: Typical work depends on detected patterns and duplicates; safeguards provide the stated worst bound.

BlockQuicksort.use: A processor-sensitive implementation where reducing unpredictable branches can justify partition buffers.
BlockQuicksort.average: Expected bounds depend on pivot assumptions; processor effects are separate from asymptotic work.

Quadsort.use: A stable merge design whose four-way merge organisation can be evaluated against ordinary two-way merging.
Quadsort.average: Depends on input structure and merge behaviour; use its implementation-specific measurements for elapsed time.

Fluxsort.use: Stable sorting where a record buffer is available and adaptive partitioning can cooperate with merging.
Fluxsort.average: Depends on how analysis divides work between stable partitioning and merging.

Crumsort.use: An unstable partitioning design when limiting workspace is more important than preserving equal-key order.
Crumsort.average: Depends on partition balance and which adaptive or fallback paths are taken.

Glidesort.use: Stable sorting of data that may offer both useful runs and repeated keys for a hybrid to exploit.
Glidesort.average: Depends on useful runs, repeated keys and the interaction between partitioning and merging.

Driftsort.use: The stable slice-sorting role described in Rust’s 1.81 release, where equal-key order must be preserved.
Driftsort.average: Depends on input order, repeated keys and the chosen small-input or hybrid path.

Ipnsort.use: The unstable slice-sorting role described in Rust’s 1.81 release, allowing equal-key order to change.
Ipnsort.average: Depends on duplicates and partition behaviour; the library’s safeguards bound adverse cases.

Bitonic sort.use: A fixed comparison schedule suited to studying parallel rounds or hardware-like comparator organisation.
Bitonic sort.average: The standard network’s comparison count is fixed by input size, independent of input order.

Odd-even merge network.use: A comparison network that should use a fixed recursive merging schedule, independent of observed key values.
Odd-even merge network.average: The fixed network performs the same comparator schedule for every allowed input of a given size.

Odd-even transposition sort.use: A nearest-neighbour model where disjoint adjacent comparisons can happen in the same round.
Odd-even transposition sort.average: A fixed-round network ignores input order; an early-exit sequential variant can do less work.

AKS sorting network.use: Understanding the theoretical possibility of logarithmic parallel depth, rather than choosing a simple practical sort.
AKS sorting network.average: Network size and depth depend on n, not on a probability distribution of input order.

Samplesort.use: Partitioning work between processors using sampled boundaries, provided buckets remain sufficiently balanced.
Samplesort.average: The expected bound depends on sampling and sufficiently balanced bucket occupancy.

IPS⁴o.use: Parallel in-place engineering where block buffers, locality and balancing work across threads matter.
IPS⁴o.average: Expected work depends on its sampling model; actual throughput also depends on processor and memory behaviour.

External merge sort.average: Depends on initial runs, RAM, fan-in and external transfers, not just an average comparison count.

Polyphase merge sort.use: A sequential-storage situation with a limited number of tape-like streams and a need to schedule merge passes.
Polyphase merge sort.average: Depends on initial run lengths, tape count and the sequence of merge passes.

Funnelsort.use: Studying cache-efficient sorting without supplying the algorithm with the cache’s specific size.
Funnelsort.average: Comparison work and expected elapsed time are distinct; its transfer guarantee uses a specified cache model.

Pancake sort.average: The basic method scans every unfinished prefix for its maximum, giving quadratic comparisons. The number and lengths of flips depend on the input.

Bead sort / gravity sort.use: A physical-model thought experiment about representing positive integers as beads and accounting for the apparatus.
Bead sort / gravity sort.average: Depends on the physical or simulated model, maximum value and representation cost.

Bogosort.use: A counterexample showing that eventually finding an answer is very different from having a practical procedure.
Bogosort.average: With independent uniform shuffles of n distinct keys, success probability per attempt is 1/n!; expected attempts are n!.

Stooge sort.use: A recursion exercise that exposes the cost of solving overlapping subproblems repeatedly.
Stooge sort.average: The standard recursion follows the same size-dependent structure regardless of input order.

Slowsort.use: A deliberate inefficiency example for learning to analyse recursive work rather than judging code by its length.
Slowsort.average: The deliberately repeated recursive structure controls its large cost; measured averages do not make it practical.

Sleep sort.average: Delays depend on values and scheduling jitter; there is no dependable general sorting-time guarantee.

Stalin sort.average: The one-pass filter performs linear work but does not preserve the full input.

I Can’t Believe It Can Sort.use: Testing an initially surprising loop structure, then explaining its correctness through an ordered-prefix invariant.

ExpoSort.use: An intentionally reluctant sorting construction used to explore exponential work rather than reduce it.
ExpoSort.average: Its deliberately exponential recursion is the object of analysis, not an optimised average workload.

LearnedSort.use: Numeric sorting where a learned estimate of rank may guide distribution and repair can restore exact order.
LearnedSort.average: Depends on the distribution, model error, training overhead and cost of repairing misplaced records.

LearnedSort 2.0.use: Studying how a learned distribution sort handles the repeated keys that challenged its earlier design.
LearnedSort 2.0.average: Depends in particular on repeated-key behaviour as well as prediction and repair cost.

AlphaDev small-sort routines.average: Input size is fixed and tiny; useful measurements compare instruction sequences on specified hardware.

DovetailSort.use: Parallel integer-sorting research in which representation and frequent keys are part of the computational model.
DovetailSort.average: Depends on the integer-key and processor model, including key frequencies.

Parameter-aware partition sorting.use: Studying a formal notion of optimality that depends on richer input parameters than length alone.
Parameter-aware partition sorting.average: Read the cited paper’s input parameters and optimality definition before comparing averages.

Adaptive Hybrid Sort.use: Examining the cited proposal’s strategy-selection rules and the assumptions behind its reported comparisons.
Adaptive Hybrid Sort.average: Depends on the specific strategies selected and the paper’s workload assumptions.
Adaptive Hybrid Sort.story: The specific research proposal linked below studies selection between strategies; this label is not a unique name for every adaptive hybrid.

bsort.use: Research on sorting different numeric representations using a binary-quicksort-derived framework.

Need for Speed Sort.use: Exploring numeric interval refinement with cleanup and fallback when an interval split does not help.

Minimal-move in-place sorting.use: Research where moving records is expensive enough to make linear moves a distinct objective.
Minimal-move in-place sorting.average: The highlighted comparison guarantee is probabilistic; it is not itself an average runtime statement.

Random-order online sorting.use: Studying the cited online arrival model; its decisions and objective differ from sorting an available array.
Random-order online sorting.average: The expectation is tied to its random-arrival model and online objective.
